documents.title: EFNS guidelines on disease management Alzheimer disease

chunks.content: 1 INTRODUCTION The prevalence of dementia in the United States is growing, and there continue to be gaps in early detection and accurate diagnosis. More than 90% of Medicare beneficiaries with mild cognitive impairment (MCI), a preceding stage of dementia, go undiagnosed. Few patients see specialty brain care providers or do so late in the disease course. However, most people in the United States receive care from a primary care provider (PCP), giving primary care (PC) the potential to play a critical role in early detection and timely diagnosis of dementia. Implementing early detection in PC is not without challenges. Lack of validated screening tools embedded into electronic health record workflows, inadequate reimbursement for cognitive assessments, limited time, insufficient training and confidence in diagnosing cognitive impairments, and limited awareness of the benefit of early interventions are all significant factors increasing the challenge for PC‐based early detection. Technological advancements, including digital cognitive assessment devices, have offered new opportunities to expand early detection and case finding. Recently demonstrated real‐world implementation of these tools in PC, , , , coupled with national and international efforts to increase PCP awareness, knowledge, and confidence in early detection, will enhance the identification of older adults with MCI and early dementia in PC practices. However, as PC‐based identification improves, it must be accompanied by coordinated diagnostic and care strategies to manage downstream impacts—particularly the growing strain on specialty care resources such as neurology and geriatrics. After identifying a cognitive concern, PCPs must guide patients through a complex array of diagnostic and treatment options. These often include referrals to geriatrics, neurology, or neuropsychology, as well as consideration of pharmacologic and non‐pharmacologic treatments and support for caregivers. The resulting care pathways are frequently fragmented and nonlinear, which can be confusing for patients, caregivers, and PCPs alike. Patient‐level factors such as multimorbidity and polypharmacy, combined with system‐level barriers such as limited access to or understanding of community resources, further challenge PCPs who attempt to facilitate early detection for their patients. As a result, patients with cognitive complaints or symptoms are frequently referred by their PCP to specialty care without a working diagnosis, further compounding challenges with long specialty care wait times and failing to match patients with the most appropriate follow‐up care and services. Addressing these dynamic barriers will require transformative changes in the culture, structure, and function of health systems, particularly through the development of robust, primary care–based pathways that support early detection and diagnosis. To date, efforts to improve detection and diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD) in PC have focused on approaches to improve the care provided by PCPs as individual care providers. However, high‐quality PC has been shown to be most effective when delivered by PC teams, with 10 principles, referred to as the “building blocks,” being recognized as the cornerstones of the patient‐centered primary care medical homes (PCMH) in the United States. Patient navigation in PC has emerged as a care model to address care fragmentation and support patients with complex needs. In PCMH settings, nurse navigators have improved chronic disease management, increased screening rates, increased patient adherence to care plans, and decreased patient anxiety. , PC navigators also provide important connections to community resources for patients and their caregivers by coordinating care across the health system continuum, resulting in high patient and provider satisfaction and improved outcomes in patients with chronic conditions (CCs). The evaluation of a patient with cognitive impairment in PC has many elements of complexity that are ideal for care navigation, including the need for review of comorbidities and medications, screening for addressable causes, and facilitation of additional testing. Improving early detection in PC has the potential to increase specialty care wait times. Improving the reliability and effectiveness of PC‐based diagnostic evaluation through nurse navigation has the potential to mitigate this effect by improving the quality of the PC evaluation and identifying the best care pathway for each patient, especially those that are most appropriate for ongoing PC management. For PC‐based early detection to be effective at a systems level, this mitigation of specialty care backlog must occur in parallel to increased detection. A care pathway connecting cognitive assessment in primary care to a navigation model has potential for both. We first introduced the Brain Health Navigator (BHN) as part of the Indiana University (IU)/IU Health site of the Davos Alzheimer's Collaborative Healthcare System Preparedness Early Detection Flagship Program in 2022. The role was created due to overwhelming feedback from PCPs that additional support was needed to facilitate the care process for patients who had abnormal cognitive screenings. , , The responsibilities and functions of the BHN were designed to facilitate the PC‐based clinical evaluation of patients with cognitive impairment, connect patients and caregivers to resources, and facilitate the patient's diagnostic and treatment pathway (Table ). We first introduced the Brain Health Navigator (BHN) as part of the Indiana University (IU)/IU Health site of the Davos Alzheimer's Collaborative Healthcare System Preparedness Early Detection Flagship Program in 2022. The role was created due to overwhelming feedback from PCPs that additional support was needed to facilitate the care process for patients who had abnormal cognitive screenings. , , The responsibilities and functions of the BHN were designed to facilitate the PC‐based clinical evaluation of patients with cognitive impairment, connect patients and caregivers to resources, and facilitate the patient's diagnostic and treatment pathway (Table ). Our successful implementation and sustainment has led to improvement in completion rates of diagnostic tests for addressable causes of cognitive impairment and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the head, as well as a higher likelihood of receiving a diagnosis of MCI than those patients who did not see the PC BHN. We argue that implementing a PC BHN using our proposed framework will be advantageous in closing known gaps in PC‐based early detection. 2 BRAIN HEALTH NAVIGATOR AND THE PRIMARY CARE MEDICAL HOME Team‐based care, patient–team partnership, care coordination, comprehensiveness, and prompt access to care represent 5 of the 10 PCMH building blocks, each of which can be built into a PC‐based early detection model. Over the past two decades, PC in the United States has undergone significant transformation toward team‐based care through the PCMH model. This shift, supported by national collaboratives and evolving payment models, has made team‐based care a key feature of many PC practices. PCMH PC teams typically consist of a “teamlet,” pairing a clinician with a medical assistant, supported by an interprofessional team that may include registered nurses, pharmacists, and behavioral health specialists. A 2019 national study found that 70% of Family Physicians reported practicing in settings that use team‐based care structures, indicating a strong foundation for integrating new roles such as the BHN. Patient–team partnership allows patients to be engaged with a team that they come to know personally. Co‐visits are a team‐based partnership model in PCMH practices where the Registered Nurse participates in the visit with the provider, and after the provider leaves the examination room, they implement the care plan. Although co‐visits are traditionally synchronous for the PCMH team and PCP, asynchronous adaptations of the co‐visit model have been successful. An asynchronous PC‐based BHN can be a pivotal team‐based solution because of the challenges of incorporating cognitive and diagnostic assessments, including time and space limitations, into PC practices. 3 BRAIN HEALTH NAVIGATOR FACILITATION OF DIAGNOSTIC EVALUATION Care coordination (the responsibility of PC teams to arrange services they cannot directly provide) and comprehensiveness (the capacity of a practice to address most patient needs) are essential components of a PC‐based diagnostic evaluation for individuals with subjective cognitive concerns or abnormal screening cognitive assessments. Although 64% of people in the United States receive their dementia diagnosis from their PCP, gaps in care coordination and comprehensiveness lead to significant variability in the diagnostic process of those patients. For example, despite recommendations for structural MRI, when imaging is ordered, PCPs are more likely to order computed tomography (CT) scans over MRI; and only 14% of PCPs report high confidence in interpreting brain imaging results. As a result, those persons with MCI and early dementia remain under‐detected, under‐diagnosed, and under‐treated in PC. An array of complex system factors contributes to these outcomes, primarily manifesting as a symptom of “time constraints.” These barriers will likely be further complicated by the integration of blood biomarkers (BBMs) into PC practices. We found previously that PCPs responded most effectively to order proposals for missing diagnostic testing compared to clinical messages recommending orders to be placed. We initially designed the PC BHN role for a Licensed Clinical Social Worker but later converted the role to a Registered Nurse, so clinical order proposals could be sent to the patient's PCP. A clinical algorithm can be used by a nurse navigator to support the PCP with laboratory and imaging result interpretation and management. In contrast to some specialty care settings, advanced practice providers, such as nurse practitioners or physician assistants, are often the patient's primary care provider, particularly in rural settings. Using an advanced practice provider as a primary care brain health navigator would, therefore, reduce the impact of a targeted facilitation of specific gaps in care by the primary care team. Thus, the PC BHN offers a system‐based solution that offers potential to enhance diagnostic clarity in the face of these challenges. 3.1 Time‐requirements Time constraints remain one of the most cited barriers to cognitive assessment in PC. Although tools such as the Mini‐Mental State Examination (MMSE) or the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), are designed to take less than 10 min to complete, they often take longer to administer in real‐world practice, especially among patients with limited health

Thus, the PC BHN offers a system‐based solution that offers potential to enhance diagnostic clarity in the face of these challenges. 3.1 Time‐requirements Time constraints remain one of the most cited barriers to cognitive assessment in PC. Although tools such as the Mini‐Mental State Examination (MMSE) or the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), are designed to take less than 10 min to complete, they often take longer to administer in real‐world practice, especially among patients with limited health literacy, which comprise up to 30% of adults is the United States. Most cognitive screening tests suitable for PC practice were developed, validated, and timed in homogenous research populations with higher health literacy and educational attainment than many PC patients. Although some tests incorporate demographic adjustments, such as educational attainment, a single cut‐point is often used to determine normal versus abnormal, leading to bias in the interpretation of the results. These limitations can contribute to educational bias, which raises the likelihood of making the screening task harder for those with low health literacy, lower educational attainment, or limited English proficiency. This can result in over‐diagnosis of MCI, if the PCP does not accurately take these moderating variables into account, which complicates the diagnostic process for PCPs. Although up to 40% of dementia cases are attributable to life‐course modifiable risk factors, the use of validated and standardized PC‐based screening scales improves the identification and detection of these addressable conditions. However, the collective time required to complete a full assessment of cognitive impairment using high‐quality validated structured tools to assess for potential addressable conditions can be substantial(Table ). Time constraints have been identified consistently as a significant barrier to PC‐based early detection, but few systems‐based approaches have been offered as potential solutions. Although a PCP may not have time in a busy clinic to complete the needed assessments, patient education, and Shared Decision‐Making (SDM), a PC BHN can provide the needed capacity for a comprehensive evaluation and care plan development. Through a coordinated nurse‐led diagnostic evaluation, the PC BHN offers an opportunity to enhance comprehensiveness of brain health evaluation in PC, by improving the quality of the PC‐based diagnostic evaluation and mitigating time constraints on PCPs. 3.2 Enhanced diagnostic clarity Up to 60% of older adults with cognitive impairment remain without a diagnosis of dementia or MCI in PC, with the majority of patients with cognitive impairment not ever being referred to a dementia specialist. Although differentiating the underlying cause of dementia often requires advanced testing, PCPs can reliably diagnose MCI and mild dementia syndrome. Nurse‐led diagnostic algorithms have been shown to be effective in facilitating diagnoses of both common and complex conditions. By guiding patients through structured, PC‐based diagnostic evaluation of cognitive concerns, a BHN can support PCPs in diagnosing MCI and mild dementia syndrome earlier and more effectively. Recommendations for clinical implementation of BBMs are evolving to include PC pathways that integrate BBMs in the evaluation of patients with cognitive concerns. Shared decision tools and workflows that further support integration into PC practices with diverse patient populations and high rates of multi‐morbidity are being developed collaboratively. As this body of work develops and evolves, the role of the BHN in facilitating patients' education and understanding of BBMs to enhance diagnostic clarity will need to be explored further, but the PC BHN BBM‐related workflows offer tremendous opportunity. The BHN model has already shown promising outcomes. In prior work, we observed increases in MCI diagnosis rates, laboratory testing for addressable causes, and MRI utilization following BHN implementation in PC practices offering cognitive screening. By improving both care coordination and comprehensiveness, the BHN can enhance diagnostic consistency, improve patient outcomes, and ensure more appropriate referrals to specialty care. 4 BRAIN HEALTH NAVIGATOR AND SHARED DECISION‐MAKING SDM is a collaborative process that respects patients’ rights to make health care choices based on their personal values and preferences. High‐quality SDM includes six key components: (1) explanation of the health care problem, (2) presentation of available options, (3) discussion of risks and benefits for all options, (4) clarification of patient values and preferences, (5) assessment of patient understanding, and (6) allowing the patient to make the decision. Higher patient‐reported health outcomes, improved quality indicators, and lower health care utilization have all been demonstrated outcomes of SDM. Health care providers widely accept the importance of these aspects of care, yet the majority of providers do not consistently use a form of structured SDM in their practice. Although lack of adequate time and concerns about increased duration of the encounter are the most cited concerns, SDM does not significantly extend visit duration. Due to these perceptions and the complexity of demands on PCPs, SDM based on physician‐driven processes

Higher patient‐reported health outcomes, improved quality indicators, and lower health care utilization have all been demonstrated outcomes of SDM. Health care providers widely accept the importance of these aspects of care, yet the majority of providers do not consistently use a form of structured SDM in their practice. Although lack of adequate time and concerns about increased duration of the encounter are the most cited concerns, SDM does not significantly extend visit duration. Due to these perceptions and the complexity of demands on PCPs, SDM based on physician‐driven processes is unreliable. The use of a clinical PC team member for SDM processes in PC is an evidence‐based solution to address time constraints, engage patients in diagnostic testing decisions and care goals, and improve outcomes in PC patients with other CCs. The role of nurse‐based SDM models related to the diagnostic, treatment, and care planning process for people with cognitive impairment and dementia has been documented as early as 1995. The use of structured tools for SDM has been found to be helpful in the context of early detection and diagnosis, and a variety of SDM tools are widely available, including tools to assist with discussions about BBMs and disease‐modifying treatments. With staff‐driven SDM processes having higher reliability, engaging clinical team members other than physicians is even more critical to the success of SDM implementation of PC‐based early detection pathways. Older adults with cognitive impairment can reliably communicate their values and choices, even when cognition declines. SDM can therefore be a powerful tool to reduce fear of loss of autonomy and increase patient engagement. A PC nurse‐based SDM approach using a PC BHN can improve the reliability and effectiveness of patient‐engaged care decisions throughout the ADRD diagnostic journey, particularly as BBM testing becomes more common in PC. 4.1 Brain health navigator connection to specialty care Even with robust PC diagnostic evaluation in PC, the connection to specialty care is a critical part of the cognitive care pathway. Yet, patients often face challenges completing these referrals. Fragmentation, related to lack of coordination and misalignment of organizational structures and systems, can lead to inefficiencies and potentially harm patient outcomes. Lack of clarity about care coordination responsibilities, long wait times for specialty care providers, geographic barriers, and concerns for cost of care are contributors to gaps of care as patients transition from PC to specialty care providers. These gaps leave as few as 40% of patients who are referred from PC to actually have a specialty care appointment. These barriers disproportionately impact patients with low health literacy and/or limited language proficiency—who are also at higher risk of over‐diagnosis of MCI—along with those patients experiencing transportation barriers and multi‐morbidity. Communication gaps, both to and from PCPs and specialists, further complicate referral pathways. For example, many PC referrals do not include a transfer of critical information to the specialist, and reciprocally, PCPs are often unnotified whether the patient was seen by the specialist. Follow‐through with specialist‐based recommendations can also be compromised by communication gaps, as the PCP may not receive follow‐up treatment plans from the specialist, necessitating reliance entirely upon the report from the patient about the specialist's recommendations. Lack of clarity about whether the referral represents a single consultation or ongoing co‐management further convolutes the relationships. These challenges in PC–specialty care referrals can contribute to missed or delayed diagnoses, delays in treatment, and other patient safety concerns. Boundary spanners are individuals who facilitate the flow of information, ideas, and resources between different groups or disciplines by functioning at the “boundary” between those groups. Effective partnerships between PC and other health care system disciplines require both sides to span the boundaries that separate them, which can be both conceptual and practical. In PC, boundary spanners often function by helping facilitate patient connections to other parts of the health care system to facilitate collaborative care. Conceptualizing the BHN role as a boundary spanner between PC and specialty care through navigation/care management holds promise to improve the over‐ and under‐utilization of dementia specialty care providers. When paired with collaboratively‐developed guidelines that identify the most appropriate care pathway for patients who have completed PC characterization and evaluation of their cognitive impairment, the BHN can play an important role in facilitating the right patients to the most effective and efficient care pathway for their individual care, thus pulling specialty care services across the boundary towards PC and making specialty care more accessible to the patients who need it most. Improved utilization of specialty care services, combined with improved quality of diagnostic evaluations in PC, has the potential to expedite access for patients who need timely referrals and in geographic areas where specialist access is particularly limited. In the era of disease‐modifying therapies, these optimized care pathways are essential to

Improved utilization of specialty care services, combined with improved quality of diagnostic evaluations in PC, has the potential to expedite access for patients who need timely referrals and in geographic areas where specialist access is particularly limited. In the era of disease‐modifying therapies, these optimized care pathways are essential to creating access to treatment. This boundary spanning function of the BHN role requires intentional implementation through partnership of PC and specialty care. Inter‐clinician relationships have been shown to have a direct impact on resource utilization and timeliness of care. Patients often identify non‐physicians, such as nurses, as key facilitators in navigating across the health care system. Building close relationships between a PC‐based BHN and the clinical care team in the memory care specialty services department is essential to successful transitions of patients who need specialty care services. 5 BRAIN HEALTH NAVIGATOR CONNECTION TO RESEARCH OPPORTUNITIES Recruitment of participants through PC has tremendous potential to enhance the real‐world validity and representativeness of ADRD clinical trials. The PC BHN can play a key role by exploring patients’ interest in research and introducing research opportunities to patients with cognitive impairment. This potential arises from a combination of factors including demographics of PC patient panels, higher rates of multi‐morbidity in PC, and success of PC practices in practice‐based recruitment for research studies. In the United States, PC patient panels closely resemble the population demographics of the communities they serve, with PC patients being slightly older and sicker than the general population. By 2050, the prevalences of hypertension, obesity, and diabetes mellitus are expected to increase beyond 60% of the U.S. adult population. The majority of patients with CCs receive care from their PCP, and PCPs deliver a disproportionate amount of the ambulatory care to disadvantaged populations in the United States. New ADRD diagnostics and treatments increase the urgency to include diverse, multi‐morbid populations in research. Significant disparities in ADRD incidence, progression, and mortality are evident across diverse racial, ethnic, gender, and geographic groups. Yet, these high‐risk groups remain markedly underrepresented in clinical trials, thereby limiting generalizability. Despite comorbidities being common in patients with Alzheimer's disease (AD), clinical trials for AD commonly have exclusion criteria related to comorbidities. CCs have been found to be related to BBM levels, yet there is a paucity of guidelines for interpretation of BBM in multi‐morbidity. Common CCs, such as diabetes mellitus and cardiovascular disease, appear to have multi‐faceted associations with AD prognostic indicators, including risk of developing AD and rapidity of progression. CCs are more common in people living with dementia (PLWD) than people who do not have dementia, complicating gaps in further evaluation of abnormal cognitive assessments. Understanding how CCs and multi‐morbidity impact patient willingness to pursue further care after an abnormal or borderline cognitive assessment is an essential aspect to offering BBMs as part of early detection in PC. Physician support for participation in research is a strong motivator for research participation. A 2020 study found that having a PCP is the strongest predictor of successful follow‐up among trial participants. PC practices can be effective in recruiting participants for clinical trials and can enhance the diversity of clinical trial populations. Practice‐Based Research Networks (PBRNs) were established in the late 1990s to designate a group of ambulatory practices devoted principally to the PC of patients and working to identify and frame research questions to improve the practice of PC. A 2007 nationwide survey of 111 PC PBRNs in the United States found that 27% provided services entirely to recruit and implement studies from investigators outside of PC and 59% of networks implemented research ideas from both PC leaders in their network and outside investigators. Over‐representation of minority and underinsured patients in PBRN practices offers promise for PC PBRN recruitment as a key strategy to enhance gaps of those populations often noted in clinical trial recruitment. Despite the complexity of recruiting subjects with cognitive impairment to clinical research, more than 40% of patients with cognitive impairment reported willingness to participate in dementia research clinical drug trials. In our implementation work, 43% of patients by a PC BHN expressed interest in research referral. By exploring patient interest in research opportunities, the PC BHN has potential to offer diverse real‐world PC patients with cognitive impairment or subjective cognitive concerns participation in ADRD research. Such a function could be tremendously valuable in creating access to research opportunities to patients who might not otherwise encounter those opportunities, and offering value to the ADRD research community by improving the representativeness of potential research subjects

In our implementation work, 43% of patients by a PC BHN expressed interest in research referral. By exploring patient interest in research opportunities, the PC BHN has potential to offer diverse real‐world PC patients with cognitive impairment or subjective cognitive concerns participation in ADRD research. Such a function could be tremendously valuable in creating access to research opportunities to patients who might not otherwise encounter those opportunities, and offering value to the ADRD research community by improving the representativeness of potential research subjects compared to the general population. 6 BRAIN HEALTH NAVIGATOR PATIENT AND CAREGIVER SUPPORT PLWD face significant challenges accessing support for their complex care needs. Disconnected system infrastructure, lack of comprehensive services to meet diverse needs, and inconsistent understanding of dementia are key gaps. PLWD without identified caregivers experience poorer quality of life and often require institutional care earlier in the course of their disease compared to those with caregiver support. Caregiving carries its own substantial burden: less than one third of caregivers report confidence in managing dementia‐related problems, less than one in five know how to access community services, and only 28% feel supported by their provider in addressing dementia‐related concerns. In the United States, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Guiding an Improved Dementia Experience (GUIDE) model launched in 2024 and is designed to reduce strain on unpaid caregivers and enable PLWD to remain in their homes and communities through an alternative Medicare payment model. Despite the large and diverse group of organizations participating in the model, many PLWD, such as those who have Medicare Advantage, and their caregivers, will be unable to access the program. The PC BHN is well positioned to provide patient and caregiver support, including connection to community resources to patients at the earliest stage of impairment and to those who do not have access to GUIDE or a similar program. Nursing interventions, across a variety of complex CCs, have demonstrated effectiveness in patient and caregiver support. PC‐based navigation support for access to community resources has been found to be satisfying to patients and resulted in more than half of patients accessing one or more community services. Despite available resources, patients and caregivers often under‐utilize support services due to lack of awareness or difficulty navigating access. , As a key team member in the cognitive assessment process, the PC BHN can identify support needs early and connect patients and caregivers with appropriate services. This proactive engagement has the potential to improve caregiver confidence, increase community service utilization, and strengthen long‐term support for PLWD. 7 BRAIN HEALTH NAVIGATOR SUSTAINABILITY Sustaining the BHN role in primary care will require alignment with evolving payment models and recognition of its value in improving patient outcomes. Although the economic impact of a PC BHN is unknown, the economic impact of patient navigator programs has been evaluated in other settings, primarily in cancer screening, and have found net financial benefit to provider practices. With patient navigation being a key aspect of PCMHs, a variety of payment models are being investigated. A 2021 report by the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine on PC called for a hybrid payment approach, including a mix of fee‐for‐service and population‐based payments, to support PC practice transformation. A 2024 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule final rule provided payment for principal illness navigation services to help patients and caregivers in care treatment for serious illnesses. This rule was viewed as providing access to care navigators and access to PC support for holistic care of patients and their families. A variety of advanced payment innovation models are being tested in the United States, which support and promote PC‐based strategies aligned with a PC BHN. Developing sustainable models of supporting PC‐based BHN services is a critical element of success for future early detection and accurate diagnosis clinical pathways in the United States. 8 CONCLUSION The PC BHN is a central and essential part of the early detection and diagnosis care team that can mitigate the time limitations of PCPs, standardize high‐quality PC‐based evaluation of cognitive impairment, and improve the appropriateness of specialty care referrals. The design of the BHN role and function should be part of the PCMH team and integrated wholly within the PC space to achieve its potential. Essential functions of a PC BHN include SDM, facilitation of brain health diagnostic evaluation, connection to specialty care, connection to research opportunities, proactive patient and caregiver education and support through the diagnostic journey, and connection to community resources. Sustainability of a PC BHN relies upon advanced payment models, including care navigation mechanisms, and requires further research and policy evaluation. Essential functions of a PC BHN include SDM, facilitation of brain health diagnostic evaluation, connection to specialty care, connection to research opportunities, proactive patient and caregiver education and support through the diagnostic journey, and connection to community resources. Sustainability of a PC BHN relies upon advanced payment models, including care navigation mechanisms, and requires further research and policy evaluation. The BHN is the linchpin necessary to enable feasibility of early detection of ADRD in PC by creating capacity and capability of the primary care team. To be effective, the PC BHN must be intentionally and contextually developed, implemented, and supported within PC and with PC leaders. documents.title: European Academy of Neurology guideline on the diagnosis of coma and other disorders of consciousness

chunks.content: 1 Introduction Disorders of consciousness refer to a category of severe neurological diseases primarily resulting from brain injury or ischemic hypoxia, leading to diminished responsiveness ( ; ). Based on standardized neuropsychological assessment scales such as the Coma Recovery Scale-Revised (CRS-R), DoC can generally be categorized into coma, vegetative state (VS), also known as unresponsive wakefulness syndrome (UWS), and minimally conscious state (MCS). Prolonged disorders of consciousness (pDoC), defined as lasting over 28 days ( ; ; ), exhibit high mortality rates; approximately 29% of pDoC patients die within 24 months post-injury, with higher mortality observed in UWS patients (42.6%) compared to MCS (16.0%), and over 65% of deaths occur within the first year ( ; ). While the precise mechanisms underlying DoC remain elusive, it’s widely accepted that disconnections in cortico-subcortical circuits are crucial ( ; ; ; ; ; ). In 2010, Professor Schiff introduced the “Mesocircuit” model, which explains neuroimaging results and therapeutic responses observed in the pathophysiological context of severe brain injuries ( ). According to this model, severe structural brain injury induces coma through either widespread neuronal death, dysfunction, or disconnection in the forebrain cortex, striatum, and thalamus, or focal lesions in the midbrain tegmentum ( ; ). Such injuries result in disinhibition of spiny neurons in GPi, leading to increased inhibition of the thalamic central lateral nucleus (CL), thereby suppressing the frontal parietal cortex. Collectively, these mechanisms contribute to downregulation of forebrain activity, causing limited or fluctuating behavioral responses ( ; ). Accumulating evidence indicates broader functions for the GPe. Empirical findings show direct connections between the GPe and cortex and thalamus. In rodent models, optogenetic manipulation and deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the GPe have been shown to enhance sleep and EEG pulse power, while cell-specific lesions of GPe neurons increase daytime wakefulness and reduce daytime non-rapid eye movement sleep ( ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ). Castillo’s case report demonstrated improved insomnia symptoms in Parkinson’s disease (PD) patients following DBS of the GPe ( ). Intriguingly, , using HARDI data from the Human Connectome Project, found probable direct connections between the GPe and prefrontal cortex and thalamus in humans. Compared to GPi, GPe exhibits distinct prefrontal and thalamic connectivity patterns, placing it at a critical location for influencing cortical electrical activity and behavioral arousal regulation. Conversely, GPi tends to connect more with motor-related areas, likely playing a greater role in motor control. The GPe might play a substantial role in the development of DoC ( ). With advances in neuroimaging, functional neuroimaging has become extensively used for diagnosing and assessing DoC. Resting-state functional imaging, due to its simplicity and versatile analytical methods, has gained popularity among researchers. This study aims to employ resting-state functional MRI, with the GPe as seed points, to investigate the relationship between the awakening state and functional connectivity of the GPe with the cortex in DoC, unveiling the neural pathways underlying arousal function in the context of DoC. 2 Materials and methods 2.1 Subjects Patients with DoC treated at the Department of Neurology, Shaanxi Provincial People’s Hospital, from November 2022 to November 2024 were recruited ( n = 50). Patients were divided into a coma group ( n = 24), a UWS group ( n = 10) and a MCS group ( n = 16). Inclusion criteria included (1) Diagnosed with coma, UWS /MCS based on the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) and Coma Recovery Scale-Revised (CRS-R); (2) Etiologies including traumatic brain injury, cerebrovascular accident, or hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy; (3) Absence of contraindications for MRI scanning; (4) No history of alcohol abuse, drug use, or psychiatric disorders; (5) No administration of sedative medications or muscle relaxants within 24 h prior to assessment. Exclusion criteria were: (1) Hemodynamic instability; (2) Contraindications to magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), included metallic implants or claustrophobia; (3) Structural MRI evidence of bilateral GPe lesions secondary to brain injury; (4) History of psychiatric disorders (DSM-5 criteria), alcohol use disorder, or substance dependence; (5) Administration of sedatives or neuromuscular blocking agents within 24 h prior to neuroimaging. Ethical approval was obtained from the Ethics Committee of Shaanxi Provincial People’s Hospital, and informed consent was signed by all participants before undergoing any procedures. 2.2 Assessment of consciousness and arousal states Participants underwent assessment using the GCS and the CRS-R for evaluating their level of consciousness ( ; ). The consciousness levels of patients were assessed by two experienced neurosurgeons three times daily during the 2 days preceding MRI scans, with the highest scores selected for diagnostic determination. The diagnostic criteria for consciousness levels in patients with DoC are summarized in ; ). In this study, the arousal state of patients was determined based on behavioral scale scores with eye-opening response evaluations. The presence or absence of eye-opening served as a key

any procedures. 2.2 Assessment of consciousness and arousal states Participants underwent assessment using the GCS and the CRS-R for evaluating their level of consciousness ( ; ). The consciousness levels of patients were assessed by two experienced neurosurgeons three times daily during the 2 days preceding MRI scans, with the highest scores selected for diagnostic determination. The diagnostic criteria for consciousness levels in patients with DoC are summarized in ; ). In this study, the arousal state of patients was determined based on behavioral scale scores with eye-opening response evaluations. The presence or absence of eye-opening served as a key diagnostic criterion for assessing consciousness levels. 2.3 Data acquisition Structural and functional MR images were acquired on a 3.0T Philips Ingenia CX scanner with a 32-channel head coil. Three-dimensional T1-weighted images were obtained using a three-dimensional fast spoiled gradient echo sequence (3D-FSPGR T1WI) with parameters: TR = 8.2 ms, TE = 3.8 ms, FOV 220 mm × 220 mm, matrix size 256 × 256, slice thickness 1 mm, no gap, number of slices 328. Resting-state fMRI data were collected using an echoplanar imaging (EPI) sequence with parameters: TR = 2000 ms, TE = 30 ms, FOV 240 mm × 240 mm, matrix 80 × 80, 200 time points, slice thickness 4 mm, number of slices 34. 2.4 Preprocessing of resting-state fMRI data In this study, the preprocessing of 3D-T1 weighted imaging (3D-T1WI) and resting-state fMRI data was conducted utilizing the DPARSF module from the Data Processing and Analysis for Brain Imaging (DPABI) toolbox (version 5.4) ( ). The preprocessing pipeline was executed using Statistical Parametric Mapping 12 (SPM12) and comprised the following steps: removal of the initial 10 time points to ensure magnetic field stabilization; temporal slice timing correction and spatial realignment of the remaining volumes; exclusion of participants with excessive head motion (mean framewise displacement >0.2 mm); coregistration of the resting-state data to 3D-T1WI templates; regression of noise components and spatial normalization to the standard Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) template; resampling to a 3 mm isotropic voxel resolution; and spatial smoothing with a 4 mm full-width at half-maximum (FWHM) Gaussian kernel. Functional connectivity analysis was performed utilizing bilateral GPe masks, derived from the HCPex template, as seed regions ( ). The specific bilateral GPe ROI mask used in this study, along with other masks (e.g., thalamus), have been made publicly available at https://github.com/XuSunAutumnFrost/GPe/tree/master . Connectivity matrices, representing seed-to-whole-brain interactions, were calculated and subsequently transformed into z-scores using Fisher’s r-to-z transformation. These z-scores quantified the strength of functional connectivity (FC) between the target brain regions and the seed areas. 2.5 Statistical analysis Statistical analyses were conducted using SPSS version 25.0 with the following protocol: Statistical data were presented as frequency (count) or percentage. Categorical data comparisons between groups were performed using the Chi-square test. Continuous data were expressed as mean ± standard deviation. Prior to group comparisons, normality (using Shapiro-Wilk test) and homogeneity of variance (using Levene’s test) were assessed. If data were normally distributed and variances were homogeneous, inter-group differences were analyzed using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA). If data were normally distributed but variances were heterogeneous, Welch’s corrected t -test was applied. For non-normally distributed data, nonparametric tests were employed. P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Etiological imbalance was analyzed using linear mixed-effects models implemented in R (version 4.5.0) with the lme4 package (version 1.1-35). The model included fixed effects for diagnosis group (coded as cerebrovascular accident (CA), Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE), or Traumatic brain injury (TBI) with CA as reference), age (continuous, in years), and gender (binary, male = 1, female = 0). To account for the hierarchical structure of the data, random intercepts were specified for two grouping factors: (1) Subject_ID to model between-subject variability, and (2) Connection_ID to model between-connection variability. Models were fitted using restricted maximum likelihood (REML) estimation. Statistical significance of fixed effects was evaluated using Satterthwaite’s approximation for degrees of freedom via the lmerTest package (version 3.1-3). Effect sizes were quantified as marginal R 2 (proportion of variance explained by fixed effects) and conditional R 2 (proportion explained by both fixed and random effects) using the performance package (version 0.11.0). Model assumptions including normality of residuals and homoscedasticity were visually inspected using diagnostic plots. Resting-state fMRI statistical analysis was performed using DPABI 5.4 ( ). FC differences among the coma, UWS, and MCS groups were analyzed. Multiple comparisons were corrected using the Gaussian Random Field method with a dual-threshold criterion (voxel-level P < 0.001, cluster-level P < 0.05). Subject-specific effects showed minimal dispersion ( ), suggesting that individual differences contributed less to overall variability than brain connection differences in this cohort (see ). 4 Discussion The globus pallidus (GP) can be anatomically, neurochemically, and functionally divided into GPe and GPi. Traditionally, the GPe has been viewed as a relay structure in the indirect cortico-basal ganglia-thalamic circuit, functioning as a node for signal transmission and modulation within neural networks, primarily supporting motor inhibition. However, recent studies have revealed its critical role in maintaining cortical electrical activity and behavioral arousal ( ; ; ; ; ). Emerging evidence also demonstrates direct GPe connections with the cortex and thalamus, implicating this structure in wake-sleep regulation ( ; ; ; ). In healthy volunteers, functional connectivity between the GP and cortex correlates with loss and recovery of consciousness during anesthesia ( ). For patients with disorders of consciousness, behavioral arousal and perturbational complexity index (PCI) - a neurophysiological measure reliably distinguishing conscious from unconscious states - show associations with atrophy severity in the GP and dorsal striatum (dSTR). Notably, over 70% of this atrophy predominantly affects the GPe according to atlas-based coordinate analyses ( ). Through high angular resolution diffusion imaging (HARDI) data from the Human Connectome Project, Zheng and Monti identified distinct connectivity patterns: the GPe preferentially connects with consciousness-related regions, particularly the prefrontal cortex and medial thalamus, participating in cortical activity modulation and behavioral arousal. In contrast, the GPi exhibits stronger connectivity with motor-associated areas, suggesting greater involvement in motor control ( ). In this study, we aim to investigate functional connectivity differences of GPe with various brain regions between patients with coma, UWS and MCS, thereby elucidating the pivotal role of the GPe in the pathogenesis of DoC. In this study, coma patients exhibited weakened FC between GPe and the left middle frontal gyrus (MFG) as well as the left superior frontal gyrus (SFG) compared to UWS and MCS group. The FC between GPe and MFG was significantly reduced by 76% in coma versus UWS ( P < 0.001), and by 73% versus MCS ( P < 0.0001). The MFG and SFG constitute the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dLPFC), a core component of the central executive network (CEN), which mediates motor tolerance, executive function, attentional allocation, emotional regulation, rewards-seeking, and memory formation ( ; ; ; ; ; ; ). Neuroimaging studies suggest the dLPFC plays a critical role in sleep-wake regulation. For instance, demonstrated via structural MRI that patients with chronic primary insomnia exhibit reduced gray matter density and volume in bilateral dLPFC, implicating these neuroanatomical abnormalities in sleep pathophysiology ( ). Functionally, hyperactivity of this region has been observed in insomnia patients. Nofzinger’s team proposed that enhanced dLPFC excitability may underlie hyperarousal to external stimuli in these individuals ( ). Additionally, research by a Chinese Academy of Sciences group revealed that the dLPFC not only encodes motor-level information accumulation during value-based decision-making but also mediates the transformation of visual features into motor signals–a process potentially modulating cortical excitability to influence arousal ( ). Non-invasive neuromodulation studies in patients with post-traumatic DoC further indicate that left dLPFC stimulation improves CRS-R scores and consciousness by enhancing theta-alpha band FC and spectral power while promoting default mode network-frontoparietal network synergy ( ; ). Intervention studies targeting the dLPFC reveal bidirectional regulatory effects: Wu et al. reported that repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS)-induced dLPFC activation significantly ameliorates sleep quality in refractory insomnia ( ), whereas Axelrod et al. found transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) over this region increases mind-wandering tendencies without altering metacognitive awareness of attentional states ( ). further elucidated this mechanism, showing that suppressing left dLPFC activity enhances task focus, suggesting its role in modulating cognitive resource allocation to regulate arousal ( ). Collectively, these findings delineate a multidimensional framework in which the dLPFC participates in sleep-wake regulation through structural, functional, and network-level mechanisms. Our experimental results demonstrated attenuated FC between the GPe and left MFG/SFG in coma patients, with these FC reductions positively correlating with arousal state, CRS-R scores, and GCS scores. Notably, the GPe-left SFG FC exhibited the strongest positive association with arousal states among all analyzed regions. Integrating these findings, we propose that diminished functional connectivity between the GPe and prefrontal regions–particularly the left SFG–may represent a potential neural mechanism underlying the dysregulation of arousal states in DoC patients. The temporal lobe, a core region for auditory and linguistic processing, plays a pivotal role in modulating consciousness states and cognitive functions across sleep stages. Notably, neuroimaging studies have revealed synchronized alterations in neural activity patterns between temporal and frontal lobes during insomnia ( ). This cortical region is particularly crucial for executive functions, actively participating in the regulation of working memory, attentional allocation, and information integration ( ). Both temporal lobe and precuneus, as key hubs of the default mode network (DMN), contribute significantly to sleep-wake regulation ( ). Our neuroimaging findings demonstrate compromised functional connectivity between GPe and left middle temporal gyrus/left precuneus in comatose patients. Importantly, these connectivity deficits showed positive correlations with patients’ consciousness levels, highlighting GPe’s potential regulatory role in maintaining arousal states. This neural circuitry alteration may underlie the pathophysiological mechanisms of consciousness impairment in comatose states. In the present study, coma patients exhibited significantly enhanced functional connectivity between GPe and CL_L and CL_R compared to UWS and MCS groups. As a pivotal component of the “Mesocircuit” model, the central thalamus is clinically and experimentally established to critically engage in consciousness recovery. Investigations of recovery in DOC reveal that increased metabolic ratios between the central thalamus and precuneus positively correlate with regained consciousness levels. Loss of afferent/efferent signaling from central lateral thalamic neurons leads to two primary consequences: (1) Prefrontal disfacilitation: Withdrawal of long-range excitation to medial frontal/prefrontal regions essential for arousal regulation (e.g., Brodmann areas 24 and 8); and (2) Striatal silencing: Reduced corticostriatal and thalamostriatal inputs to striatal medium spiny neurons (MSNs), resulting in decreased MSN firing rates, disruption of basal ganglia throughput, and ultimately, compromised conscious states ( ; ). Neuroimaging and electrophysiological studies substantiate the central thalamus’s role in DOC recovery. Structural pathology analyses demonstrate that thalamic and basal ganglia integrity predicts restoration of awareness and wakefulness, while functional imaging confirms preserved central thalamic metabolism and structural connectivity in recovering patients. Critically, our observed GPe-CL hyperconnectivity may reflect pathological over-inhibition within the “Mesocircuit” model. As proposed by , the GPe modulates cortical and thalamic activity through: Direct GABAergic projections to frontal cortices; Inhibitory control of thalamocortical relay neurons ( ). demonstrated that patients with DoC, particularly those diagnosed with UWS, exhibit disruption in the structural-functional network repertoire. This impairment is characterized by reduced dwell time and loss of nonstationarity in the subcortical fronto-temporoparietal network (Sub-FTPN) ( ). Critically, the Sub-FTPN incorporates key subcortical nodes, including the thalamus, and its dysfunction underscores the pivotal role of thalamocortical connectivity in the pathophysiology of DoC and consciousness recovery ( ). These findings provide empirical support for the “Mesocircuit” model. demonstrated that pathological and pharmacological low-level states of consciousness exhibit disrupted phase-synchronization patterns, characterized by reduced connectivity, increased segregation, and diminished temporal recurrence compared to conscious states. These alterations co-occur with decreased global network coupling and loss of heterogeneity in regional dynamics, leading structural hubs (including subcortical regions such as the thalamus) to shift from stable noisy oscillations toward unstable oscillatory regimes near the bifurcation point ( a j ≈ 0). Crucially, this loss of hub stability contributes to the breakdown of the core-periphery architecture, highlighting the pivotal role of thalamocortical hubs in maintaining consciousness ( ). This is mechanistically consistent with the strong negative correlation between GPe-CL_L connectivity and behavioral arousal levels (rs = −0.86, P < 0.001). Collectively, these findings extend the “Mesocircuit” model, implicating dysregulated GPe-thalamocortical circuitry as a neural substrate for suppressed arousal in DOC. Our study revealed diminished FC between GPe and right precentral gyrus in coma patients compared to the UWS /MCS group. The precentral gyrus, housing the primary motor cortex, is principally responsible for voluntary movement control ( ). Previous investigations have established that GPe participates in motor regulation through parvalbumin-positive (PV+) neurons and NPAS1+/FOXP2+ neuronal projections to the subthalamic nucleus (STN) and dorsal striatum (dStr) ( ). The observed FC between GPe and the right precentral gyrus in our findings suggests potential direct or indirect anatomical connections between these regions that might contribute to motor coordination. However, as this investigation primarily focuses on the relationship between GPe and arousal states in disorders of consciousness (DOC), detailed exploration of motor-related neural circuits falls beyond our current research scope and warrants further dedicated investigation. Our findings revealed a pronounced left-hemispheric lateralization, with the majority of significantly altered functional connections localized to the left hemisphere. While functional lateralization is well-established in the human brain ( ), its characterization within the basal ganglia, particularly in DoC, remains limited ( ; ; ). The precise functional significance of this lateralization is incompletely understood, though it likely plays critical roles in both physiological and pathological processes. The left-lateralized pattern of impaired functional connectivity observed in DoC patients may be associated with two key considerations: First, the left hemisphere’s established role in integrative functions such as language and motor control ( ) could render its networks more susceptible to disruption in consciousness disorders. Second, inherent lateralization of GPe structural connectivity, as reported in human and animal studies ( ; ), may predispose left-hemispheric circuits to functional alterations. However, due to the modest cohort size and the lack of subgroup analyses based on lesion location, definitive conclusions regarding the causal role or universal significance of this lateralization in DoC cannot be drawn. Future investigations with larger, stratified cohorts are essential to elucidate the impact of hemispheric lateralization on consciousness impairment and recovery trajectories. While our results demonstrate functional correlations between GPe and specific cortical regions, the existence of direct anatomical connections and precise neural circuitry requires validation through tractography studies and electrophysiological approaches. This study primarily aims to elucidate GPe’s regulatory role in maintaining arousal states in DOC patients through comprehensive analysis of cerebral functional networks. By identifying key brain regions functionally connected to GPe and reconstructing potential neural pathways, we seek to establish a theoretical framework for developing novel neuromodulation strategies targeting consciousness restoration. Building on this framework, future research should investigate the therapeutic efficacy of targeted neuromodulation applied to the functionally significant regions identified in this study. Specifically, TMS directed at the left superior frontal gyrus, or DBS targeting the bilateral GPe/CL, could be evaluated. Assessing the impact of such interventions on consciousness recovery would provide critical empirical validation of our model and potentially offer novel avenues for arousal enhancement in patients with disorders of consciousness. 5 Limitations Several limitations should be acknowledged in this investigation. First, the relatively small sample size may limit the generalizability of our findings. Future investigations should employ larger cohorts to validate GPe-related network alterations across DOC subtypes. Second, the assessment of arousal states relied exclusively on clinical scales (CRS-R), which carries inherent subjectivity. Subsequent studies should incorporate quantitative electrophysiological biomarkers (e.g., EEG-derived consciousness indices) to objectively verify arousal levels. Third, the unavailability of MRI data from demographically-matched healthy controls restricts the interpretation of the observed FC alterations in relation to normative brain connectivity patterns. Future studies should include matched healthy control data to further elucidate functional connectivity configurations in the DoC brain. To address these constraints, we recommend implementing longitudinal follow-ups with standardized treatment protocols and initiating multicenter collaborative studies. Such methodological enhancements would enable rigorous characterization of FC abnormality trajectories and their predictive value for consciousness recovery. 6 Conclusion In patients with DoC, we observed significantly diminished FC between GPe and cortical regions–specifically the left middle frontal gyrus, left middle temporal gyrus, left superior frontal gyrus, left precuneus, and right precentral gyrus–alongside enhanced FC between the GPe and bilateral CL. These aberrant connectivity patterns primarily implicate three core neurocognitive networks: executive control, default mode, and primary motor networks. Critically, FC strength between the GPe and these dysconnected regions positively correlated with arousal levels, with GPe-left superior frontal gyrus connectivity demonstrating the strongest association (rs = 0.61, P < 0.001). Conversely, GPe-CL connectivity exhibited significant negative correlations with arousal (left: rs = −0.86; right: rs = −0.55; P < 0.001). Collectively, these findings reveal: (1) Segregated cortico-subcortical connectivity: Disrupted GPe-cortical decoupling coexists with pathological GPe-thalamic hyperconnectivity in coma.
